rows.text: Source A tells me that residents can vote from 1 to 14 March, online or at the booth beside the market, and that every household has one vote.

The message is that residents now have real power over how the money for the estate is spent. The poster says 'This year YOU decide how $500,000 is spent' and promises 'The projects with the most votes will be built'. The capital letters and the firm promise show that the choice belongs to the residents and not to the council. It is speaking to every household in the estate. It wants them to believe that their vote counts, so that they take part.
Source B is a resident speaking at a meeting and Source C is a letter from an elderly resident. Both are about the vote on the budget.

They are similar in showing that residents who organised their neighbours got their project. B says 'we knocked on doors, got our neighbours to vote, and it came first'. C says 'The blocks with young families and big chat groups got what they wanted'.

C says 'The blocks with young families and big chat groups got what they wanted'. They are different on whether the vote gave residents a say. B says 'the people who use the path decided'. C says 'I learnt about the vote only when I saw workmen at the playground', so the writer had no say at all. They also differ in purpose. B is proud and wants the meeting to see the vote as a win for ordinary residents, so the speaker sets 'the people who use the path' against 'an office that has never walked it in the rain'. C is upset and wants the council to see who was left out, so the letter points to the 'broken ramp' that 'got 41 votes and nothing'.
Source D is reliable because it is from the yearly report of the town council. The town council ran the vote, so it knows what happened.

Source D is reliable. It says '2,140 households took part' and 'All three winning projects were completed on time and within budget'. These are clear facts and figures, so it shows the vote was a success.

Source D is not fully reliable. It calls the vote 'a great success' because '2,140 households took part'. But Source E says only 'One in seven households voted', and among residents aged 70 and above only 'one in twenty'. D also says 'Residents have told us they feel heard', yet the writer of Source C 'learnt about the vote only when I saw workmen at the playground'. The check shows that D is right about the number but leaves out how few and how uneven the voters were. So it cannot be fully trusted as evidence of success.

Source E is useful. It shows that the vote did not speak for the whole estate: 'Among households with children, one in four voted; among residents aged 70 and above, one in twenty'. So the decisions followed what some groups wanted. It can be trusted. The researchers are not part of the council, they 'surveyed 600 households', and they report both a weakness and a strength: the winners were 'within 300 metres of the blocks that voted most', yet 68% called the vote 'a fairer way to decide than before'. Source C supports it: an elderly writer says 'nobody told us at Block 230'. It is limited in one way. It tells us who voted, not whether the projects were what the estate needed most. So it is very useful for showing whose wishes the decisions followed, and less useful for judging the projects themselves.

I agree to some extent. Source B shows the vote got something done that residents had wanted for years: 'For six years we asked for a covered walkway' and this time 'it came first'. Source D also agrees. It says 'All three winning projects were completed on time and within budget', so the decisions were carried out well. Source C disagrees. The writer 'learnt about the vote only when I saw workmen at the playground', and the ramp that 'wheelchair users need every day' got nothing, so a real need was missed. Source F also disagrees: urgent repairs 'will never win a popularity contest', so a vote leaves out what is necessary.

Source F also disagrees: urgent repairs 'will never win a popularity contest', so a vote leaves out what is necessary. The sources that disagree are stronger. D is the council praising its own scheme, and B speaks for the group that won. C is only one resident, but Source E backs the letter: among residents aged 70 and above only 'one in twenty' voted, and the winners were 'within 300 metres of the blocks that voted most'. F is an engineer who knows the estate and still grants that the new projects 'are well used', so that view is balanced. So I agree only to a small extent: the vote chose things residents liked, but better decisions would also have covered the needs of those who did not vote.
